content: Otitis media with effusion (OME), commonly referred to as glue ear, is characterized by the accumulation of fluid in the middle ear without signs of acute inflammation or infection. It is the most frequent cause of acquired hearing loss in children and a common reason for the surgical insertion of ventilation tubes, also known as grommets. Various treatments have been proposed for OME, including decongestants, mucolytics, steroids, antihistamines, and antibiotics. Autoinflation devices, which are mechanical tools designed to improve middle ear ventilation, have been suggested as a potential non-invasive treatment option. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of autoinflation compared to no treatment in both children and adults diagnosed with OME. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, and others, for both published and unpublished randomized controlled trials. The most recent search was completed on April 12, 2013. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized controlled trials that compared any form of autoinflation to no autoinflation in individuals with OME. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted relevant data. A total of eight studies, involving 702 participants, met the inclusion criteria. The overall quality of the studies was assessed as having a low or unclear risk of bias, with the unclear risk primarily attributed to insufficient reporting of details. Importantly, there was no evidence of selective reporting across the studies. The pooled data from these studies suggested that autoinflation was generally favored as an intervention. However, it did not demonstrate a statistically significant effect on tympanometry results (type C2 and B) within one month or beyond one month of treatment. Similarly, no significant improvements were observed in discrete pure-tone audiometry or non-discrete audiometry outcomes. When a composite measure of tympanometry or audiometry was analyzed, autoinflation showed a non-significant trend toward benefit within one month, but the effect became statistically significant after more than one month of treatment (Relative Risk Increase [RRI] 1.74, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 1.22 to 2.50). Subgroup analysis revealed that the use of a Politzer device, a specific type of autoinflation tool, had a significant effect on outcomes. For treatment durations under one month, the RRI was 7.07 (95% CI 3.70 to 13.51), and for durations over one month, the RRI was 2.25 (95% CI 1.67 to 3.04). Importantly, none of the included studies reported a significant difference in the incidence of side effects between the intervention and control groups. The authors concluded that while the included studies were small, of limited treatment duration, and had short follow-up periods, autoinflation appears to be a reasonable and low-cost option for managing OME while awaiting its natural resolution. The absence of adverse effects further supports its consideration in clinical practice. Primary care settings may serve as an appropriate environment to evaluate the utility of autoinflation devices, and ongoing research in this area is warranted. Future studies should focus on the optimal duration of treatment, the long-term developmental outcomes in children, and additional quality-of-life measures for both children and their families.
